routes.description: Jesus identifies himself with the second divine power depicted in Jewish scripture, while his followers' worship, prayer, and divine-name practices confirm that identification.
routes.successCriteria: Show that Jesus' sayings and actions are best explained as personal divine self-identification rather than merely delegated authority, and answer the strongest agency-based readings.

motionBridge.description: The relevant texts are best explained by Jesus personally claiming divine identity.

centralBridges.description: First-century Jewish two-powers traditions make a distinct yet divine Son coherent.
Jesus' Johannine sayings identify him uniquely with the Father and divine prerogatives.
Jesus' Daniel 7 trial claim presents him as the divine cloud-riding Son of Man.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The reactions of opponents and followers illuminate what Jesus communicated about himself.

routes.description: The texts portray Jesus as God's uniquely exalted agent who bears the divine name and exercises conferred authority without personally identifying as Yahweh.
routes.successCriteria: Provide coherent agency-based readings of the central sayings and reactions, while showing that blasphemy accusations and high christology do not establish Jesus' own divine claim.

motionBridge.description: Delegated authority and divine name-bearing better explain the relevant evidence than personal divine identity.

centralBridges.description: A non-Yahweh agent may bear God's name and authority without being Yahweh.
John's unity and I-am language permits non-identity readings grounded in context and agency.
The trial's blasphemy charge does not securely establish a claim to be Yahweh.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Hostile reactions are unreliable guides because misunderstanding is a recurring narrative theme.
Later exaltation and worship can concern authority conferred by God rather than intrinsic identity.

sections.title: Two Powers or Divine Agency
sections.rationale: This foundational dispute determines whether scriptural distinctions within divine appearances support Jesus' identity or instead supply a model of authorized representation.

proMoves.speaker: David Wood
proMoves.proposition: Jesus' primary divine claim was to identify himself as one of the two divine powers already visible in Jewish scripture.

sourceSpan.excerpt: And then Jesus came along and he says in effect, you know those two powers that you've been reading about in the scriptures, you know those two powers that you're so confused by? I can tell you about those two powers because I'm one of them. That's the primary way Jesus claims to be God.

proMoves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Wood's uninterrupted opening statement after his explicit introduction by the moderator.

response.rationale: This is an opening constructive statement of the affirmative's governing interpretive framework and therefore has no earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two-powers thesis and its application to Jesus are recoverable, though the precise sense of distinct divine power remains partly implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical conclusion is stronger than this summary span alone, which announces rather than yet completes the supporting textual case.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is intelligible, but it depends on the still-unproved bridge from two divine figures to Jesus' intended self-identification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies a textual framework but compresses the historical representativeness and the application warrant at this point.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive opening, it directly establishes the affirmative's principal route and the claim the later debate contests.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially advances the declared central bridge connecting Jewish two-powers traditions to Jesus' identity claim.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops its own position without representing or attacking a live opposing alternative.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: The move relies on Wood's preceding survey of passages depicting two distinguishable figures described as the Lord or acting with divine status.

conMoves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
conMoves.proposition: Jewish divine-name investment allows agents to exercise God's authority without being Yahweh, furnishing a better explanation of Jesus' status.

sourceSpan.excerpt: But this idea of the divine name being invested into people and them having the authority of God without being Yahweh themselves is I think the important ticket here.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The passage occurs in O'Connor's uninterrupted rebuttal and explicitly answers Wood's divine-identity framework.

components.text: The two-powers evidence specifically warrants identifying Jesus as divine rather than as an authorized agent.
The proposed framework is historically representative of how Jesus' claims would have been understood.

response.rationale: The name-bearing model directly contests the inference from divine authority to identity, but this short move does not independently settle the historical prevalence of either framework.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between possessing divine authority and being Yahweh is explicit and consistently stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The phrase 'I think' appropriately presents the agency model as an interpretive judgment rather than a demonstrated necessity.

charity.alternative: Wood argues that Jewish two-powers material identifies Jesus as a distinct but genuinely divine figure.
charity.decisiveQualification: The contrary model preserves genuine divine authority while denying that bearing it entails being Yahweh.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The identity-authority distinction supplies a coherent rival explanation without contradicting the acknowledged elevation of Jesus.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The broader rebuttal supplies examples, but this selected formulation still compresses how representative the name-bearing mechanism was.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive identity inference but leaves the affirmative's historical two-powers framing only partly answered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con route's central name-bearing bridge as an alternative explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: It preserves the affirmative's claim that Jesus exercises divine authority while contesting only the further inference to identity.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor supports the distinction with Jewish name-bearing traditions and subsequently invokes Josephus and conferred-name language.

sections.title: Unity with the Father in John
sections.rationale: John's claims that Jesus and the Father are one and mutually indwell each other are central evidence, while their extension to believers creates a direct interpretive challenge.

proMoves.speaker: David Wood
proMoves.proposition: The disciples' worship, prayer, doxologies, and liturgical treatment of Jesus show that a merely creaturely reading makes Jesus an implausibly poor communicator.

sourceSpan.excerpt: He's careful about what he's saying and sometimes he unveils things in different ways. But when he makes a point, seems people get this point. If all of his followers just seem to misunderstand him and start worshiping him and praying to him, making doxologies for him and so on, putting their liturgy around him, then you're saying Jesus was just a terrible, terrible communicator.

proMoves.attributionBasis: The span is the conclusion of Wood's rebuttal immediately before applause and the moderator's transition to O'Connor.

components.text: Jesus uses the same unity and indwelling language for believers, weakening an identity inference from that language.

response.rationale: The reception argument bears on whether Jesus communicated divinity, but it does not directly explain the extension of unity language to believers.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reception-based proposition is clear, but 'all of his followers' overgeneralizes the available evidence and alternatives.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Early devotional practice is probative, but the move treats widespread reception as nearly excluding development or misunderstanding.

charity.alternative: O'Connor argues that Jesus is an exalted agent and model of unity with God rather than God himself.
charity.decisiveQualification: That view need not claim every follower simply misunderstood Jesus; it can allow later development and differentiated devotional meanings.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument is plausible but moves too quickly from early reception to what Jesus personally and unambiguously communicated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several devotional phenomena are named, though their dating, distribution, and inferential connection to Jesus' own claim remain compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: It offers contrary evidence about reception but does not contact the selected target's decisive textual analogy.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It advances the subsidiary reception bridge rather than directly resolving the central meaning of John's unity language.

representationalCharity.rationale: Framing the alternative as requiring all followers to misunderstand Jesus omits possibilities of development and differentiated agency.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: The move cites prayer, worship, doxology, and liturgical practices directed toward Jesus as cumulative evidence of communicated status.

conMoves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
conMoves.proposition: Jesus' unity and mutual-indwelling language cannot by itself establish identity with God because John applies the same relational pattern to believers.

sourceSpan.excerpt: What does Jesus say in his own words? John 17 20 onwards. My prayer is not for them alone, the disciples. I pray also for those who believe in me through their message, that all of them may be one. Father, just as you are in me and I am in you, may they also be in us. This is crucial.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span occurs during O'Connor's opening statement and is presented in his sustained discussion of John 10 and John 17.

response.rationale: This is the con side's constructive textual argument about Johannine unity language and has no earlier selected target in this section.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison is textually bounded to unity and indwelling language and does not claim that every Johannine status claim is identical.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited parallel strongly supports the limited conclusion that this language alone does not entail numerical or ontological identity.

charity.alternative: The affirmative treats 'I and the Father are one' and mutual indwelling as intense evidence of Jesus' divine identity.
charity.decisiveQualification: The argument challenges sufficiency of that language rather than denying Jesus' unique role or elevated status.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The same-author comparison establishes a strong defeater to an unqualified inference from unity language to identity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies a specific textual parallel and the relevant comparative wording, with only broader contextual distinctions left compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive, it clearly presents the central con-side reading that the affirmative must overcome.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con route's central bridge concerning Johannine unity and agency.

representationalCharity.rationale: It recognizes the language as christologically intense while precisely contesting the inference drawn from it.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: The evidence is the explicit John 17 comparison between Father-Son unity and the requested unity of believers with them.

sections.title: The I-Am Saying and Name-Bearing
sections.rationale: The debate directly contests whether John 8:58 invokes God's name and, even if it does, whether invocation establishes identity rather than authorized representation.

proMoves.speaker: David Wood
proMoves.proposition: Jesus' followers calling on his name as they call on Yahweh's name supports treating Jesus as divine rather than merely as a name-bearing intermediary.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Calling on the name, calling on the name of Yahweh. And Paul sees the Christians calling on the name of Jesus. Why is this so important? You have Christians calling on the name of Jesus as they call on the name of Yahweh.

proMoves.attributionBasis: The span occurs in Wood's rebuttal, identifiable from the surrounding sustained response to O'Connor's name-bearing argument.

components.text: The Septuagint's abbreviated divine name is ho on rather than ego eimi.
Even deliberate divine-name invocation may signify delegated representation rather than identity.

response.rationale: Parallel invocation of Jesus and Yahweh directly pressures the agency model, but it does not answer the lexical Septuagint objection or fully exclude authorized mediation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The asserted devotional parallel is clear, while the exact theological implication of 'calling on the name' remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The parallel is significant but does not by itself eliminate every Jewish agency or mediation account.

charity.alternative: O'Connor allows divine-name language for Jesus while explaining it through authorized name-bearing.
charity.decisiveQualification: Name-bearing can include extraordinary devotional and authoritative functions without straightforward identity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The devotional parallel is a coherent inference to elevated divine status, though identity remains an implicit further bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A concrete early-Christian practice supports the move, but comparative Jewish agency evidence is not resolved within it.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive agency question but leaves the lexical argument about ego eimi unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the subsidiary reception bridge rather than independently completing the motion-level claim.

representationalCharity.rationale: It engages the actual name-bearing alternative, though it understates how much authorized invocation that view may permit.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: The move relies on the early Christian practice of invoking Jesus' name in a manner Wood compares with scriptural invocation of Yahweh.

conMoves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
conMoves.proposition: Ego eimi is not itself the Septuagint's abbreviated divine name, and even an intended name allusion could indicate delegated name-bearing authority.

sourceSpan.excerpt: In the Greek Septuagent, the abbreviation of the divine name is not ego Amy. It's Hon. And it's ego Amy that Jesus says. But supposing for a moment that this really were an invocation of the divine name, I'm just willing to grant it. There is a tradition in early Jewish texts of endowing beings who are not Yahweh with Yahweh's name and thereby enabling them to exert his authority.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span is within O'Connor's uninterrupted opening treatment of John 8:58 and early Jewish name-bearing.

response.rationale: The move constructively supplies both a lexical objection and a concessive agency account of divine-name invocation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The lexical and concessive arguments are separately identifiable, and the claim is carefully limited to what name invocation can establish.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move expressly grants the disputed allusion for argument's sake and advances agency as a live explanatory alternative.

charity.alternative: The affirmative reads 'before Abraham was, I am' as deliberate invocation of God's revealed name and hence divine self-identification.
charity.decisiveQualification: The con argument grants possible intentional invocation while denying that invocation necessarily entails identity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The two-stage argument remains effective even if the initial lexical objection is rejected because the agency alternative is independently stated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Septuagint wording and Jewish name-bearing practice provide specific support, though the latter's applicability to Jesus needs fuller comparison.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive, it anticipates and answers both the lexical and theological forms of the divine-name inference.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central name-bearing bridge underlying the con route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move tests the strongest opposing reading by granting intentional divine-name invocation before presenting its alternative consequence.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: O'Connor compares the Septuagint wording of Exodus 3 with ego eimi and invokes early Jewish traditions in which non-Yahweh agents bear Yahweh's name.

sections.title: Daniel 7 and the Blasphemy Charge
sections.rationale: The trial saying is the clearest Synoptic exchange bearing on Jesus' own claim, and the debate sharply contests whether the charge proves a Yahweh identification.

proMoves.speaker: David Wood
proMoves.proposition: Jesus identifies himself at trial with Daniel's cloud-coming Son of Man, and the immediate blasphemy verdict indicates a perceived divine claim.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The high priest asked him are you the Christ the son of the blessed and Jesus said I am and you will see the son of man seated at the right hand of power and coming with the clouds of heaven. The high priest tore his garments and said what further witnesses do we need, you have heard his blasphemy. How many powers in heaven? I see two here.

proMoves.attributionBasis: The passage is part of Wood's uninterrupted opening argument, combining his quotation of Mark 14 with his stated inference.

response.rationale: This is the affirmative's opening construction from Jesus' trial saying and the high priest's reaction, without an earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The textual claim and reaction are clear, although the inference from blasphemy to divine identity depends on an implicit legal-historical premise.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conjunction of cloud imagery and the charge is substantial evidence, but the move treats the charge's meaning as less contestable than shown later.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The textual sequence creates a stable inference, with the meaning of the blasphemy charge as the principal unresolved bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move uses a specific trial passage and its immediate narrative reaction, though broader legal and interpretive context is compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive, it clearly establishes one of the affirmative's most direct routes from Jesus' words to the motion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central Daniel 7 bridge and nearly reaches the motion, while still relying on the reaction inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move constructs its own case without representing a developed opposing alternative.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: The evidence consists of Mark's trial saying, cloud-coming and enthronement imagery, and the reported immediate charge of blasphemy.

proMoves.speaker: David Wood
proMoves.proposition: A merely messianic claim would not explain the death-worthy blasphemy response, whereas identifying the cloud-rider as Yahweh does.

sourceSpan.excerpt: If he's just thinking of the son of man coming with the clouds of heaven as the Messiah, then this guy claimed to be the Messiah. But it's not this blasphemy sort of thing. It sounds like it's talking about Yahweh when the ancient of days is Yahweh. It doesn't seem like they were taking that to just be a claim to be the Messiah.

proMoves.attributionBasis: Turn-taking and the proposition identify this as Wood's response, though the ledger contains no explicit speaker labels at this dialogue point.

components.text: The argument presupposes that the high priest already interpreted Daniel's Son of Man as Yahweh.
Blasphemy could cover offenses other than personally claiming to be Yahweh.

response.rationale: Wood argues that the reaction itself favors a divine interpretation over a merely messianic one, but does not eliminate the wider range of possible blasphemy offenses.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast between merely messianic and Yahweh-level readings is clear, though the range of legally possible charges remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reaction favors Wood's interpretation, but the warrant does not establish it without stronger evidence about the priest's assumptions.

charity.alternative: O'Connor argues that the inference requires an implausibly specific prior interpretation by the high priest.
charity.decisiveQualification: O'Connor does not reduce the saying to an ordinary self-description; he allows messianic and corporate readings of Daniel 7.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative inference is coherent, but it does not exhaust alternative grounds for a blasphemy accusation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The narrative reaction supports the inference, while direct evidence of the high priest's Daniel interpretation remains unavailable.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive presupposition challenge but leaves the broader scope of blasphemy charges unresolved.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly defends the affirmative's central Daniel 7 bridge against its strongest objection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately engages the priest-interpretation objection, though it compresses the con side's alternative legal explanations.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: The reply compares the expected consequences of an ordinary messianic claim with the reported capital blasphemy response.

conMoves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
conMoves.proposition: Using the blasphemy charge to prove divine identity presupposes, without evidence, that the high priest already interpreted Daniel's Son of Man as Yahweh.

sourceSpan.excerpt: If your position is correct and that is the only thing that he could have been accused of blasphemy for, then you have to presuppose that the high priest had that interpretation of Daniel 7, which just seems so implausible to me, that they thought at that time that this son of man would be Yahweh himself.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The adversarial wording and turn sequence attribute the response to O'Connor, but the ledger does not explicitly label the speaker here.

components.text: Cloud-coming and enthronement imagery itself identifies Jesus with Yahweh.
The high priest's blasphemy response establishes that Jesus was understood to claim divine identity.

response.rationale: The move directly attacks the decisive reaction-based inference but does not independently resolve the force of the cloud-coming imagery.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional nature of the objection and the precise disputed presupposition are explicitly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The objection identifies a real evidential gap, although calling the priestly interpretation implausible is not fully supported within this move.

charity.alternative: Wood argues that the capital blasphemy reaction is best explained by a perceived claim to be Yahweh.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection accepts the conditional force of that reasoning if divine identity were the only possible basis for blasphemy.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The presupposition challenge is logically focused and exposes a necessary historical bridge in the reaction argument.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The missing-evidence diagnosis is useful, but the positive claim of implausibility receives limited historical support in this span.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive blasphemy component while leaving the independent cloud-rider argument unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the affirmative's central Daniel 7 bridge rather than assuming a positive contrary burden.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move states the affirmative reasoning conditionally and targets its strongest necessary presupposition without caricature.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: The objection rests on the absence of direct evidence for the high priest's specific interpretation and the existence of other historical readings of Daniel 7.
